analysis.one_liner: Delays by one year new consumer protections for prepaid debit cards.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, died in the House Financial Services Committee without a vote, so the prepaid card rule took effect on its original schedule.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2016 the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau finalized a rule requiring prepaid debit cards to disclose fees clearly, limit overdraft-type fees, and protect funds if a card is lost or stolen. This bill would have pushed the rule's start date back by one year, to October 2018, giving card issuers more time to comply. The bill never left committee and never got a vote, so the rule proceeded as scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Prepaid card issuers and the banks and payment companies behind them. They would have gained an extra year without having to meet the new disclosure, fee, and fraud-protection requirements, delaying compliance spending on upgraded systems and customer disclosures.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prepaid card issuers and payment companies

how_it_helps.text: Postpones the effective date of the CFPB's prepaid account rule from October 1, 2017 to October 1, 2018, and pushes the deadline for issuers to submit account agreements to the Bureau from 2018 to 2019 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People who use prepaid cards — disproportionately lower-income and unbanked consumers — would have continued for another year facing fee schedules that were not clearly disclosed and weaker protections against losing money to fraud or error.
analysis.who_pays_short: Prepaid card users, mostly lower-income consumers

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs are real: card issuers would have had to update disclosures, fee structures, and error-resolution systems by the original deadline, and one year less lead time raises those costs [S2][S3].

Some issuers argued the rule was finalized close to its compliance date, leaving little runway for smaller providers; supporters of a delay made exactly this case, though no cosponsors joined [S1][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A one-year delay would have modestly lowered compliance costs for card issuers, but at the price of another year of unclear fees and weaker fraud protections for the lower-income consumers who rely on prepaid cards. The trade favored the industry over the users, and the bill died before those costs fell on anyone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never came up again, dying when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Tipton introduced the PACER Act on March 30, 2017, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services, where it stayed for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
The committee never marked it up, the House never voted on it, and the bill expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prepaid card users came out ahead: the consumer protections took effect as scheduled instead of being delayed a year. Issuers had to bear the compliance costs the bill would have postponed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prepaid card users, not the issuers

for.name: Rep. Scott Tipton
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill to delay the CFPB prepaid card rule by one year.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no cosponsors and no votes ever occurred, so no party split can be measured; the House Financial Services Committee simply never acted on it [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Prepaid card issuers and payment processors
industries.note: The bill would have given them an extra year before fee-disclosure, overdraft-fee limits, and fraud protections applied, delaying compliance costs at the expense of cardholders' clarity and safety.
